div.p: Your Majesty’s servant Shang Han, grandson of the King of the Central Mount, in Lew Chew, respectfully memorializes the throne, requesting that he be confirmed in his succession to the princely station, which will at once encourage him in his loyalty, and render illustrious the statutes of the empire.

Your servant is well aware that his little state lies in the far distance, and is only like a foot of ground for size, yet even away in mid-ocean it has an established government, and during successive generations its rulers, having received investiture, have here guarded the frontiers.
I look up to the imperial benevolence, vast and expanded beyond expression, and am profoundly sensible that all here are unable adequately to express our thanks.

My remote ancestor, Shang Chi, was indebted to the favor of the Emperor Shun Chi for conferring on him the dignity of King, in A. D. 1655, and granting him a royal seal, which constituted him King in the Middle Mount, and forever tranquillized his maritime feudality.
His successor, Shang Ching, was indebted to the letters patent and proclamation of the Emperor Kang-hi, who, in the year A. D. 1683, thereby constituted him the King.
His son, Shang Shun, died when he was the heir; and the next in succession, Shang Yih, deceased before he could apply for and receive investiture.

The next was Shang King, who, through the bedewing favor of the same Emperor, was confirmed in his seat in the year 1719. At the same time the deceased Shang Yih was retrospectively recognized as having been legitimate King.
Your servant’s high progenitor, Shang Muh, recently received investiture in the year 1757, from the Emperor Kien Lung.

His son, Shan Cheh bade adieu to this world while still heir-apparent, and left the succession to his son, Shang Wan, who, by the high favor of Your Imperial Majesty, was installed as King in the Middle Mount in the year 1801, and fulfilled the duties of his princely station with reverence and diligence One morning he fell sick, and the remedies of the physicians were powerless to arrest his disease; he departed on the long journey in August, 1803.
Your servant’s father, Shang Ching, had no opportunity to ask investiture, for he suddenly left the world; and I, a mere youth, am called on to succeed to his post and take the inheritance.

As the obligations of a feudal prince are strict, I dare not style myself so without authority. Therefore, to perpetuate the kingly power and observe the requirements, I now request Your Majesty’s investiture. I shall then be able to salute your decree in this sea-girt spot, where I keep ward over your frontier, and bow down before your command in this wave-worn corner of your realm, whence I can send up my tribute and my reverence.
I have now specially commissioned my personal minister, Yang Kih Tien, with the councilor Liang Pang Pih, who are to hasten to the vermilion ante-room to hand in this memorial request.

Humbly prostrating myself, I look up to ask that the sacred kindness may grant to me, as it was granted to my predecessors, that an imperial envoy be sent here to perform the ceremony of installing me in my kingly dignity.

On Your Majesty’s part, such an act will render more illustrious the fullness of the statutes. On my part, it will invite me to more reverence and obedience in every particular. It will, no doubt, strengthen this remote possession for generations to come, and, honored by the crowning blessing, Your Majesty’s favor will continue through succeeding ages unimpaired.

I humbly implore the penetrating glance to rest upon my memorial, and beg that the proper board may be required to carry my desire into effect. Your servant will await the arrival of these orders in trembling expectancy, and now carefully prepares his memorial for your imperial hearing.

closer.dateline: Dated in the reign of Kia-King, 11th year, 8th moon, 7th day (or about September 1, 1809).
